issue.issue_text: Whether the power of the Custodian under section 12 to cancel a lease is limited by the non-obstante clause to only overriding statutory bars, and not the contract under which the lease is held.

facts: The appellants, who held a lease from the Custodian of evacuee property, were issued a notice to show cause why their lease should not be cancelled.

The appellants argued that the Custodian's power to cancel the lease under Section 12 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act was limited by the section's non-obstante clause, which reads "notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force".
They contended that this clause meant the Custodian could only override statutory laws, but not the terms of the contract (the lease) itself.
law: The operative portion of a statutory section grants the primary power and its plain meaning should be upheld.
A non-obstante clause is typically inserted "ex abundanti cautela" (out of an abundance of caution) to repel possible contentions that the section is overridden by other laws.
A non-obstante clause cannot be construed to cut down or abridge the plain meaning and scope of the main, operative portion of the section.
application: The Court found that the operative portion of Section 12, which grants the Custodian the power to cancel or vary the terms of a lease, is "unqualified and absolute".

It reasoned that the non-obstante clause was not intended to limit this absolute power. Instead, its purpose was to prevent any argument that other statutes conferring rights on lessees could override the Custodian's authority under Section 12.
The Court further noted that the section's express power to "vary the terms of the lease" is inconsistent with the idea that the Custodian is bound by the original contract and cannot go back on it.
Therefore, the Court concluded that the non-obstante clause could not be used to abridge the clear and absolute power granted to the Custodian in the main part of the section.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellants' argument, holding that the Custodian's power to cancel a lease under Section 12 is unqualified and absolute. The non-obstante clause does not limit this power to only overriding statutory bars; rather, it was included to ensure the Custodian's power prevails over any conflicting laws and cannot be used to diminish the plain meaning of the power granted by the section.

issue.issue_text: Whether the operative portion of section 12, which confers power on the Custodian to cancel a lease, is unqualified and absolute.

facts: The Custodian of evacuee property granted a lease to the appellants.
Subsequently, the Custodian issued a notice to the appellants to show cause why the lease should not be cancelled.
The appellants challenged the Custodian's authority, arguing that the power to cancel a lease under section 12 of the Act was limited.
law: Section 12 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, states that "notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, the Custodian may cancel any... lease..."
The appellants contended that this "non-obstante clause" meant the power could only be used to override a bar imposed by another law, but not the terms of the contract under which the lease was held.
application: The Supreme Court rejected the appellants' argument, finding it to be "without any substance."
The Court held that the operative portion of the section, which grants the Custodian the power to cancel a lease, is the primary source of authority and its meaning is plain.

It explained that the non-obstante clause ("notwithstanding anything contained in any other law...") was not intended to limit this power. Instead, it was inserted "ex abundanti cautela" (out of an abundance of caution) to prevent a possible argument that other statutes protecting lessees' rights would override the Custodian's power.
The Court reasoned that this precautionary clause could not be interpreted to "cut down the plain meaning of the operative portion of the section."

Furthermore, the Court noted that the section also expressly authorizes the Custodian to "vary the terms of the lease," which is inconsistent with the idea that the Custodian cannot go back on his own contracts.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the operative portion of section 12, which confers power on the Custodian to cancel a lease, is unqualified and absolute. This power is not abridged or limited by the non-obstante clause.

issue.issue_text: Whether a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution for a writ of habeas corpus is maintainable for an alleged detention by a private person.

facts: The case involved a petition for a writ of habeas corpus filed under Article 32 of the Constitution.
The petition was directed against a private person (a father) for the alleged detention of another private person (his daughter).
law: A petition under Article 32 of the Constitution can be entertained by the Supreme Court only for the enforcement of fundamental rights.

The fundamental right under Article 21 (protection of life and personal liberty) is a protection against actions by the State or under the authority of the State, not against actions by private individuals.
application: The Court reasoned that since the alleged detention was by a private person and not by the State, there was no infringement of any fundamental right under Article 21.
Because no fundamental right was infringed, the primary condition for invoking the Supreme Court's jurisdiction under Article 32 was not met.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that it will not entertain an application for a writ of habeas corpus under Article 32 when the detention is by a private person. Consequently, the petition was not maintainable and was rejected.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the power of the Custodian under section 12 to cancel a lease is limited by the non-obstante clause to only overriding statutory bars, and not the contract under which the lease is held.
appellant_arguments: The Custodian's power to cancel a lease under section 12 could be exercised only to override a bar imposed by any law, but not the contract under which the lease is held.

This limitation flows from the language of the non-obstante clause, which is limited to 'anything contained in any other law for the time being in force', and does not include 'or any contract between the parties'.
respondent_arguments: The operative portion of section 12, which confers power on the Custodian to cancel a lease, is unqualified and absolute.

The non-obstante clause is intended to repel a possible contention that section 12 does not by implication repeal statutes conferring rights on lessees, and it cannot be construed as cutting down the plain meaning of the operative portion of the section.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the operative portion of section 12, which confers power on the Custodian to cancel a lease, is unqualified and absolute.
appellant_arguments: The power of the Custodian is not unqualified and absolute, as it is limited by the non-obstante clause to overriding statutory bars and not contractual terms.
respondent_arguments: The operative portion of section 12 which confers power on the Custodian to cancel a lease or vary the terms thereof is unqualified and absolute.

This power cannot be abridged by reference to the non-obstante clause, which was inserted 'ex abundanti cautela' (out of abundant caution) and does not cut down the plain meaning of the operative part of the section.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The power conferred by the operative portion of a statutory section is unqualified and absolute and cannot be abridged by reference to a non-obstante clause. A non-obstante clause is inserted out of abundant caution to repel a possible contention that the section does not by implication repeal other statutes, and it cannot be construed as cutting down the plain meaning of the operative portion of the section.
obiter: A contention not put forward at any stage prior to the hearing of an appeal would be sufficient ground for declining to entertain it.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court's central finding is that the operative portion of a statute, which confers a power, is unqualified and absolute unless expressly limited. A non-obstante clause, such as 'notwithstanding anything contained in any other law', should not be interpreted as cutting down or limiting the plain meaning of the operative part. Instead, such a clause is typically inserted 'ex abundanti cautela' (out of abundant caution) to clarify that the power overrides conflicting statutes, not to restrict the power's application to only those statutory conflicts.
legal_tests_applied: The principle of statutory interpretation that the operative portion of a section, which confers a power, is unqualified and absolute and cannot be abridged by reference to a non-obstante clause.

The rule that a non-obstante clause is often inserted 'ex abundanti cautela' to repel a possible contention that the section does not by implication repeal other statutes, and it should not be construed as cutting down the plain meaning of the operative part of the section.

A petition for a writ of habeas corpus under Article 32 of the Constitution is not maintainable for detention by a private person, as the fundamental right under Article 21 is a protection against the State, not private individuals.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument that the Custodian's power was limited by the non-obstante clause was rejected because the court found the operative portion of section 12, which grants the power to cancel or vary a lease, to be unqualified and absolute.

The court found the appellant's interpretation to be inconsistent with the express authority given to the Custodian to 'vary the terms of the lease', which is irreconcilable with the idea that he cannot go back on his own contracts.
The court refused to construe the non-obstante clause as a source of limitation, viewing it instead as a tool to ensure the Custodian's power prevailed over other laws conferring rights on lessees.
The court also noted as a procedural defect that the appellant had not raised this specific contention at any stage prior to the appeal.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's argument that the operative portion of section 12 is unqualified and absolute was accepted by the court.

The court agreed with the respondent's characterization of the non-obstante clause as having been inserted 'ex abundanti cautela' to repel possible contentions about conflicting statutes, rather than to limit the Custodian's primary power.

The court's interpretation, supported by precedent, was that the plain meaning of the operative part of the section could not be cut down by the non-obstante clause, thus upholding the respondent's actions.
